public_rationale: In July 2025 Veracode tested more than 100 LLMs on 80 security-sensitive coding tasks. It found vulnerabilities in 45% of cases, and security performance was not improving as models got better at writing working code. A December 2025 Carnegie Mellon benchmark of coding agents on real-world tasks found the best setup's solutions were 61% functionally correct but only 10.5% secure. Both studies predate the post and show that the security of AI-generated code was seriously in doubt. A July 2026 Veracode follow-up found little change, which is consistent with this but came after the post.
limitations: The main studies are a vendor report and a preprint (later accepted at ICML 2026). Both use test tasks, not audits of deployed code.
'Very much in question' is qualitative. The studies show serious doubt, not that all AI code is insecure.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: as of the post (February 2026), credible evidence showed AI-generated code often contains security vulnerabilities, so its security could not be taken for granted.
Ongoing-state claim with no named period. The target period is the half-year before the post, which covers the most recent major security studies published before it.
This does not require that all AI code is insecure. It requires that substantial, documented security doubts existed.
criteria.support_condition: Credible studies published in the period find substantial vulnerability rates in code written by LLMs or coding agents.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Credible studies in the period find that AI-generated code from current models is generally secure, for example with vulnerability rates comparable to or below careful human code and no serious documented concerns.

evidence.excerpt: The study analyzed 80 curated coding tasks across more than 100 large language models (LLMs), revealing that while AI produces functional code, it introduces security vulnerabilities in 45 percent of cases.
evidence.explanation: A large test across more than 100 LLMs found vulnerabilities in 45% of cases. That is a substantial documented security problem in AI-generated code.

evidence.excerpt: Although 61% of the solutions from SWE-Agent with Claude 4 Sonnet are functionally correct, only 10.5% are secure.
evidence.publisher: arXiv (Zhao et al., Carnegie Mellon University)
evidence.explanation: On real-world feature tasks, a frontier coding agent produced secure solutions only 10.5% of the time. The authors say this raises 'serious concerns' about vibe coding.

evidence.excerpt: roughly 44% of AI code generation tasks introduced a risky security vulnerability in tests. The average security pass rate across models is 56% – barely changed from 55% in the first report.
evidence.explanation: Published after the post. It shows the concern persisted, with roughly flat security pass rates. Context only.
